strengths: The paper presents a well-motivated and systematic representation study comparing BEV tokens against perspective-image tokens for LLM-based spatial reasoning in driving, with a thoughtful set of baselines (majority class, region-aware linear probe, and a UniAD detection head) that control for dataset bias — a rigor often missing in VQA-style evaluations.

The cross-view experiments on Ego3D cleanly demonstrate the central hypothesis: BEV tokens substantially improve LLM spatial reasoning (e.g., +46% MCQ accuracy over ViT tokens without fine-tuning) while using a 10x smaller visual encoder and fewer tokens, and the analysis of the confound introduced by BEV fusion parameters is honest and largely convincing.

The semantic distillation framework is evaluated on a closed-loop, safety-critical benchmark (NeuroNCAP) rather than only open-loop L2, which is the right evaluation choice given known open-loop/closed-loop discrepancies; the ablations on VQA data types (Behavior/Planning > Perception/Prediction) and impact-velocity analysis give meaningful insight into why distillation helps.

Experimental coverage is broad: two VLM families (InternVL3, DeepSeek-VL), two LLM scales (1B/8B), ablations on token downsampling, and honest failure-case analysis (Appendix D.2), plus a clear limitations discussion including computational cost and the human-curated VQA dependency.
Reproducibility support is good: detailed implementation, tokenization counts, coordinate conversion, training schedules, and explicit acknowledgment of licenses/public resources used.
weaknesses: Generality is limited: all distillation and closed-loop results use a single BEV encoder architecture (BEVFormer/UniAD) and a single data ecosystem (nuScenes/DriveLM). The authors acknowledge this due to compute cost, but the claim that BEV is a 'superior scene representation' for LLMs would be much stronger with at least one alternative BEV encoder or dataset.

The closed-loop gains, while directionally meaningful, are modest in absolute terms: the 8B variant reaches a NeuroNCAP score of 2.71/5 (baseline 2.10), collision rate only drops from 62% to 55%, and the 1B variant leaves collision rate essentially unchanged (0.62 -> 0.63). The 29% headline improvement is a relative score gain on a benchmark where even the improved model collides over half the time; more statistical analysis or variance estimates would strengthen the claim.

The representation comparison carries a residual confound the paper does not fully resolve: BUniAD comes from an encoder already trained with supervised 3D detection annotations, so its spatial advantage over a raw ViT may partly reflect geometry-aware supervised training rather than the BEV format itself. The 10% parameter argument addresses capacity, but not this supervision asymmetry.

The 'first rigorous representation study' claim is somewhat overclaimed given concurrent/related work connecting BEV and language modalities (e.g., BEV-LLM [4], BEVDriver [62], HERMES [77]), which the paper cites but positions as insufficiently systematic without fully justifying the distinction.

The distillation formalization (Sec. 4.1, Eq. 1) is more rhetorical than technical: v* is never concretely defined, and the actual method reduces to VQA-driven fine-tuning of the BEV encoder with a frozen LLM and joint detection loss — the 'semantic manifold' framing adds narrative but little operational novelty over standard auxiliary VQA training; a comparison against simply adding a VQA task head (auxiliary supervision) is missing.

Several evaluation sets are small: the Ego3D object-centric test distribution spans only 162 questions (e.g., 42 absolute-distance MCQs, 43 numerical), so the reported 46% accuracy improvement has wide confidence intervals; no significance testing is provided.

No code release is mentioned, and open-ended generation metrics (BLEU ~0.47, CIDEr ~3.7) show only modest absolute quality, suggesting the distilled encoder's open-vocabulary semantic capability remains limited.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly written: the paper identifies a genuine gap (BEV representations are spatially consistent but semantically impoverished relative to VLM vision encoders) and structures the work around three explicit research questions.

The representation study is designed with unusual care for confounds: majority-class and linear-probe baselines control for dataset bias, a detection-based rule baseline isolates projector quality, and spatial filtering of DriveLM questions is documented in the appendix.

Closed-loop evaluation on NeuroNCAP (in addition to open-loop L2 on nuScenes) is the right choice for a safety claim, and the impact-velocity / crash-severity analysis plus qualitative corner-case studies add depth beyond a single score.
Reasonable ablations: BEV token downsampling methods, VQA data subsets (behavior/planning matter most), and LLM teacher scale (1B vs 8B).
Limitations and broader impact are discussed honestly, including compute constraints, single-architecture choice, and the reliance on human-curated VQA data.
weaknesses: The headline claim of a '46% improvement' over multi-view inputs is overstated by the paper's own Table 3: the fair comparator, IViT w/ fine-tuning, achieves 62.18 avg MCQ accuracy vs. 61.34 for BUniAD — the BEV representation is actually slightly *worse* than a fine-tuned ViT on cross-view reasoning. The 46% figure is computed against the unfine-tuned IViT baseline, which is not an apples-to-apples representation comparison.

The Ego3D evaluation, on which the cross-view claim largely rests, is very small: Table 8 shows only 162 testing questions total (e.g., 42 for object-centric absolute-distance MCQ). Gains of this size on samples of tens of questions are statistically fragile, and no significance testing, confidence intervals, or multiple seeds are reported anywhere.

Single-view gains on DriveLM are marginal (90.8 vs. 90.3 for BUniAD vs. IViT with projector; IUniAD is slightly lower), so the practical significance of the representation study is thin outside the small Ego3D set.

The 'distillation' framing is more rhetorical than technical: Eq. (1) reduces to cross-entropy VQA training of the BEV encoder with a frozen LLM attached via an MLP projector — essentially standard VLM-style auxiliary supervision, not knowledge distillation from the LLM in any meaningful sense. The 'semantic manifold' narrative does not correspond to a distinct mechanism.

The claimed mechanism (LLM semantics transferred into the BEV encoder) is never directly validated: no before/after distillation VQA or reasoning accuracy for the distilled encoder is reported. The NeuroNCAP gains could plausibly stem from additional training data/iterations rather than any LLM-derived semantics; a control using VQA supervision without the frozen LLM (or extra detection-only epochs) is missing.

E2E gains are modest and mixed: open-loop L2 improves by only ~0.08m, collision rate for the 1B distilled model is unchanged/slightly worse (0.62→0.63), and the 8B improvement (0.62→0.55 collision rate, 2.10→2.71 score) is from a single run with no variance estimate on a simulation benchmark.

Generality is limited: only one BEV architecture (BEVFormer/UniAD), one VQA dataset (DriveLM-nuScenes), and one E2E pipeline are tested; architectural generality is deferred to future work on compute grounds, which weakens the claimed significance of the framework.

Contribution type (not declared, treated as Algorithms/General): the individual components (MLP projector alignment, auxiliary VQA loss, multi-task retention) are all established techniques; the novelty lies mainly in the empirical comparison, whose evidential weight is undermined by the issues above.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and timely question: whether spatially consistent BEV representations are better inputs for LLM-based spatial reasoning in driving than independently tokenized multi-view images. The systematic representation study (ViT tokens vs. UniAD backbone tokens before/after BEV fusion) is a useful contribution that isolates the representational effect reasonably carefully, including controlling token counts (2,250 vs. 2,500) and discussing the extra-parameter confound of the BEV fusion module.

The semantic distillation framework is simple and practical: freezing the LLM as a fixed semantic teacher, jointly training the BEV encoder with VQA and detection objectives, and evaluating the distilled encoder in a standard E2E pipeline (UniAD) preserves deployment relevance. The connection between LLM-aligned BEV features and downstream closed-loop safety is an interesting and non-obvious finding.

Evidence is layered and covers both open-loop (nuScenes L2) and closed-loop (NeuroNCAP) evaluation, which is appropriate given known limitations of open-loop planning metrics. The closed-loop gains (NeuroNCAP score 2.10 -> 2.71, collision rate 62% -> 55%, lower impact velocities) with qualitative velocity-profile and corner-case analyses are the strongest part of the empirical case.

Ablations are thorough: LLM scale (1B vs. 8B teacher), VQA data subsets (showing Behavior/Planning questions matter most), downsampling/projector design, and full per-class results in the appendix. Two LLM backbones (InternVL3, DeepSeek-VL) support generality of the representation findings.

The manuscript is clearly written and well organized around three research questions. The supplementary material provides substantial implementation detail, data filtering procedures, example questions, failure-case analysis, explicit licenses/attribution of all public resources, and an honest limitations discussion (single BEV architecture, computational cost, reliance on human-curated VQA data).
weaknesses: The framing 'distilling semantic knowledge from LLMs' is somewhat overstated. The supervision signal comes from human-curated DriveLM ground-truth answers; the frozen LLM acts mainly as a differentiable decoder/teacher head. The paper lacks a decisive control experiment isolating whether LLM-specific knowledge (beyond generic VQA multi-task training) matters, e.g., distilling via a small non-LLM QA model or direct answer-token supervision without the LLM. The Behavior/Planning subset ablation partially addresses this but does not disentangle it fully.

Generality of the main claim is limited to a single BEV encoder architecture (BEVFormer/UniAD). Given that the paper argues 'BEV should serve as a superior scene representation' as a general conclusion, experiments with at least one alternative BEV encoder would substantially strengthen the case; the computational-cost justification for deferring this is understandable but leaves a core claim weakly supported.

Several quantitative claims need more care: the headline '46% improvement' is a relative gain on a small Ego3D MCQ subset (162 test samples total), and in Table 3 the fine-tuned ViT baseline (IViT w/ ft.) actually achieves a higher average MCQ accuracy (62.18) than BUniAD (61.34), with only the L1 distance favoring BEV. The single-view DriveLM gains (e.g., 90.8 vs. 90.3 vs. 89.8) are within ~1% with no variance or significance reported; all experiments appear to be single runs.

The absolute closed-loop performance remains low (NeuroNCAP score 2.71/5), and the safety gains, while consistent, are demonstrated only on one simulation benchmark with one E2E pipeline. A variance estimate or multiple seeds would be important given the relatively modest margins in the open-loop and DriveLM results.

Efficiency claims in the abstract/introduction (redundant computation of independent view processing, temporal cost trade-offs) are motivators but are never quantified with inference-time or memory measurements for BEVLM vs. multi-view token baselines.

Novelty positioning is somewhat strong: recent works on connecting BEV and language (e.g., BEV-LLM [4], BEVDriver [62], HERMES [77]) are cited but the claimed 'first rigorous representation study' could be stated more carefully relative to these concurrent efforts. The distillation objective in Eq. (1) is also informal (v* is undefined operationally beyond the cross-entropy proxy).

strengths: Well-structured paper with clearly stated research questions (RQ1-RQ3) that logically build from representation alignment, to a comparative representation study, to semantic distillation and closed-loop driving evaluation.

The representation study (Sec. 3) is a valuable empirical contribution in itself: carefully controlled comparison of BEV tokens vs. image tokens (I_ViT, I_UniAD, B_UniAD) using the same backbone and matched token counts, with sensible baselines (majority class, region-aware linear probe, UniAD detection head) that rule out dataset-prior explanations.

Strong experimental practice on the safety side: closed-loop NeuroNCAP evaluation with mean±std over 50 random seeds, and a thoughtful analysis showing that the score gains mostly reflect reduced crash severity (impact velocity analysis in Appendix D.3), including an honest failure case (Fig. 7).

Good ablation and control design: the randomly initialized auxiliary head baseline (Tab. 4) convincingly isolates the contribution of the pretrained LLM's semantics vs. simply adding a VQA head; comparison against a VLM-AD-style CLIP-space distillation addresses the most relevant alternative; downsampling and VQA-data-type ablations add further insight.

Comprehensive appendix with implementation details (tokenization counts, dataset filtering, coordinate conversion, training configs) that supports reproducibility; limitations are candidly discussed (single BEV architecture, human-curated VQA data, computational cost).
Gains generalize across two E2E pipelines (UniAD and VAD) rather than a single architecture, supporting the claim that distilled BEV encoders are broadly useful.
weaknesses: The headline 46.0% cross-view reasoning improvement is measured on a very small evaluation set: Tab. 8 shows only 162 Ego3D test samples (object-centric questions: 42+34+43 MCQ + 43 numerical). Relative improvements of this size on such small samples can be noisy; no statistical significance or confidence analysis is provided.

On DriveLM single-view reasoning, the BEV advantage is marginal (e.g., 90.8 vs. 89.8-90.3 for the 1B model in Tab. 2a; 90.5 vs. 91.1 with encoder fine-tuning in Tab. 10 reverses the ordering). The paper's framing as 'BEV is a superior scene representation' rests disproportionately on the small Ego3D benchmark.

Absolute closed-loop gains are modest and high-variance: UniAD 2.38→3.05 (std ±1.26 vs. ±1.52) and collision rate 0.56→0.47±0.30; VAD improvements are smaller (3.24→3.42, 0.37→0.34). With stds of this magnitude, the significance of the CR reductions is unclear and should be quantified.

A potential confound is not fully ruled out: the distilled encoder receives one extra epoch of training on DriveLM VQA (including planning-relevant supervision), while the baseline freezes the BEV encoder. The random auxiliary head partially controls for this, but a control with equivalent additional training/budget (e.g., continued detection-only fine-tuning) would strengthen the causal claim that it is LLM 'semantics' rather than extra supervision/data that drives the gains.

The 'distillation' framing (Eq. 1, the v* semantic manifold interpretation) is loose; in practice this is VQA-based multi-task fine-tuning of the BEV encoder through a frozen LLM cross-entropy loss, and Eq. 1 is only an approximation. The conceptual novelty over multi-task supervision is real but narrower than the framing suggests.

Generality is limited to one BEV encoder family (BEVFormer/UniAD/VAD lineage); the authors attribute this to computational cost, but for a paper whose central claim is about BEV representations in general, at least one alternative encoder would materially strengthen the evidence.

The claim of being 'the first' to compare image- vs. BEV-based inputs for LLM reasoning should be softened given cited works (BEV-LLM, BEVDriver, HERMES) that connect BEV and language; the genuinely novel part is the systematic controlled comparison plus distillation, not the connection itself.

Qualitative NeuroNCAP results (Fig. 4, 6) are selected examples; only one failure case is shown, and the transferability of safety gains beyond the NeuroNCAP scenario distribution (generated from nuScenes) is unknown.
Evaluation relies solely on nuScenes-derived data (DriveLM, Ego3D, NeuroNCAP); cross-dataset or cross-domain generalization of the distilled encoder is not examined.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly written representation study: the paper systematically compares image tokens (IViT, IUniAD) against BEV tokens (BUniAD) for LLM spatial reasoning, controlling for token count, encoder size, and projector, which is a genuinely useful empirical contribution to the community (Contribution 1).

The central claim is supported by controlled experiments across two LLM families (InternVL3, DeepSeek-VL) at two scales (1B/8B), with sensible baselines (majority class, region-aware linear probe, task-specific detection head) that guard against dataset-prior explanations for the accuracy gains.

The semantic distillation framework is simple, well-specified (Eq. 1, training details in Appendix A), and evaluated with meaningful ablations: downsampling/projector variants (Tab. 5), VQA data subsets (Tab. 6), and importantly a random-auxiliary-head control and a VLM-AD-style comparison (Tab. 4) that help attribute the closed-loop gains to pretrained LLM semantics rather than the auxiliary supervision itself.

Closed-loop evaluation on NeuroNCAP with 50 random-seed runs, plus analysis of impact velocity and honest failure cases (Appendix D.2), is a stronger and more honest evaluation protocol than open-loop-only comparisons.
The limitations section and appendix (E.2) are candid about single BEV architecture, dependence on a human-curated VQA dataset, and computational constraints.
weaknesses: Generality of the framework is demonstrated on essentially one BEV encoder family (BEVFormer/UniAD/VAD share the same encoder), which weakens the claim that the gains 'generalize across BEV-based architectures'; the computational-cost justification for not testing other encoders is understandable but leaves the strongest version of the claim unsupported.

Statistical support for the headline closed-loop gains is questionable: NeuroNCAP score improvements of 2.38±1.52 → 3.05±1.26 (UniAD) and 3.24±1.21 → 3.42±0.97 (VAD) have overlapping standard deviations, and the VAD collision-rate change (0.37→0.34) is small; no significance testing is provided, so the '28.2% improvement' headline rests on a gain smaller than the reported variance.

Much of the safety improvement is a reduction in collision severity (impact velocity) rather than collision rate on UniAD (0.56→0.47, largely unchanged for the 1B variant), which is a more modest and harder-to-interpret safety claim than the framing in the abstract suggests.

The cross-view reasoning evaluation (Tab. 3) rests on a very small test set (162 Ego3D questions, e.g., 43 localization MCQs); the '46.0% improvement' headline number is computed on this small sample, and no confidence intervals are given.

The comparison between modalities is imperfectly controlled: the Ego3D 'IViT w/ ft.' fine-tuning protocol and the extra parameters of the BEV fusion are discussed, but the potential benefit of BEV features already being supervised with geometric 3D ground truth (detection pretraining) versus an untuned ViT confounds the representation story; the authors' argument is plausible but not fully verified (e.g., a geometrically supervised image-space encoder baseline is missing).

Distillation supervision depends on ground-truth-derived coordinate conversion and human-curated DriveLM QA, which limits practical applicability; the paper acknowledges this but the practical value claim ('real-world value') is overstated relative to this dependency.

Novelty relative to concurrent BEV+LLM works (BEV-LLM [4], BEVDriver [60], HERMES [75]) is discussed only briefly; the 'first rigorous representation study' claim needs a sharper differentiation from these closely related efforts.

Open-loop L2 gains are small in absolute terms (Avg. L2 1.05→0.97 UniAD, 0.82→0.74 VAD) and, as the authors themselves note, open-loop metrics are weak evidence; the paper is appropriately self-critical here but this limits the strength of Tab. 4.
